newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds soar on mild inflation, dollar dips.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds soar on mild inflation, dollar dips.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks ended slightly higher Wednesday after soaring with bonds on news that inflation remained under control.
The dollar tumbled to its lowest level against the yen in nearly four months on rumours that the U.S. Treasury would support a stronger Japanese currency.
Coffee prices soared to their highest level in 11 years on news that Latin American supplies are tight and U.S. inventories of high quality beans are at 20-year lows.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 11.95 points at 7,286.16, which was just shy of Monday's record finish of 7,292.75.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,473 to 993 on active volume of 489 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Blue chips romped ahead from the start with the Dow surging more than 75 points on news that the Producer Price Index for April posted its biggest drop in nearly four years, falling 0.6 percent.
The Labour Department's report signalled an economy that continues to grow with few signs of outright inflation.
It was the fourth straight month that producer prices have fallen and followed a 0.1 percent slide in March.
Analysts said the big drop in the producer prices lowered the odds that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates at next Tuesday's policy-setting meeting.
But investors turned cautious and took profits, realising that a good producer price report did not necessarily bode for a similar consumer price figure.
"When you get these oddball moves in PPI, they're not usually replicated in CPI. It takes a lot more to tug CPI from its underlying trend," said Fred Sturm, economist at Fuji Securities Inc.
Economists expect the CPI to show an April increase of 0.1 percent after a similar rise in March.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond jumped half a point, or $5 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.88 percent from Tuesday's 6.93 percent. The bond's price and yield move in opposite directions.

"If (Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan) wants to be pre-emptive against inflation and sneak some tightenings in before the next downturn, he's going to do it even if this week's data is benign," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer of Value Line's Asset Management division.
Although some Wall Streeters may be bracing for another rise in interest rates next week, analysts remain confident that the Fed is not about to embark on a long-term cycle of rate increases.
The dollar sank briefly to 116.95 yen, a level not seen since mid-January.
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 117.23 yen, down from 118.67 yen late Tuesday. The dollar fetched 1.6947 German marks, up slightly from 1.6940 marks.

At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for May delivery rose to a new life-of-contract high at 270.00 cents a pound and closed up one-half cent at 261.50 cents, the highest closing price since March 1986.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices led grains lower as speculators bailed out of the market. Soybeans for May delivery fell 11-1/4 cents a bushel to close at $8.69.
Soybeans hit an 8-1/2 year high at $9.03-1/2 on May 7.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly prices rose on news that meatpacker IBP Inc. would cut back the hours at its Midwest slaughter plants due to poor profit margins. Pork bellies are used to produce bacon.
Pork bellies for May delivery rose 1.425 cents a pound to 87.375 cents.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed 4.1 points lower at 4,686.9. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 closed up 80.61 points or 0.40 percent at 20,209.72.
